title: Modeling the Impact of Climatic Variables on Cotton Production in Pakistan: Evidence from VAR and Deep Learning (LSTM, RNN, GRU) Models
abstract: This study investigates the impact of key climate variables (temperature, rainfall and CO2 emission) on cotton yields in Pakistan by using data of 1961-2022. Researchers used vector auto regression (VAR) model and advanced neural network methods such as LSTM, RNN and GRU. The VAR results revealed only limited immediate causal relationships between climate indicators and cotton output based on non-significant Granger tests and subdued impulse responses. However, these variables were found to play an increasingly important role in long term variability in production using forecast error variance decomposition. In training, the deep learning models were good; the lowest in-sample error (RMSE 0.10) was for GRU. However, when applied to new, unused data, all models had less accuracy because of over-fitting. The findings highlight the need for adaptive measures in relation to the agriculture sector in Pakistan, particularly in major cotton growing regions such as Punjab, to reduce the growing climate risks and the economic sustainability.
problem: Previous research on climate's impact on Pakistan's cotton production relies on linear models that are insufficient to explain the complex, non-linear dynamics and dynamic interdependencies between climatic variables and crop output, while long-term systematic evidence remains limited.
method: This study proposes a hybrid framework combining Vector Autoregression (VAR) with deep learning models (LSTM, RNN, GRU) to investigate the linear and non-linear impacts of climate variables on cotton production in Pakistan.
task: The task is to model the impact of climatic variables on cotton production in Pakistan by comparing the performance of a Vector Autoregression (VAR) model with deep learning models (LSTM, RNN, and GRU).

Table 3 gives an overview of the diagnostic tests of the estimated VAR model. The results of the Granger causality suggest that cotton production is largely self-driven and there are no high results of short-run causality of climatic variables. Ljung-Box test confirms the presence of no autocorrelations in most equations but there are some slight problems in the rainfall equation. Jarque-Bara test indicates the violations of normality in the equations of CO2 and cotton, whereas ARCH tests indicate evidence of homoscedasticity. Stability diagnostics depict slight instability, which means that the outcomes are more accurate with respect to short-term analysis.

These findings demonstrate the efficiency and strength of GRU in terms of computation that is applicable in agriculture time-series data.
